query: Under Philippine law, is a clinical or psychiatric evaluation mandatory to prove psychological incapacity for the declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code? Cite the controlling jurisprudence.

sources.title: AIDA EGMALIS-KE-EG vs. REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES
sources.text:
Psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code as a ground for declaration of nullity of marriage

 The psychological incapacity of a spouse is a ground for declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code which states:

 Art. 36. A marriage contracted by any party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential marital obligations of marriage, shall likewise be void even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after its solemnization.

 "Psychological incapacity" was first explained inSantos v. Court of Appeals44(Santos) wherein the Court declared that the clear intendment of the law was to confine the meaning of the term to "the most serious cases of personality disorders clearly demonstrative of an utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage." The psychological condition must exist at the time of the celebration of the marriage.45

sources.title: G.R. No. 143376 (Supreme Court Decision)
sources.text: "It should be obvious, looking at all the foregoing disquisitions, including, and most importantly, the deliberations of the Family Code Revision Committee itself, that the use of the phrase psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Code has not been meant to comprehend all such possible cases of psychoses as, likewise mentioned by some ecclesiastical authorities, extremely low intelligence, immaturity, and like circumstances (cited in Fr. Artemio Baluma's Void and Voidable Marriages in the Family Code and their Parallels in Canon Law, quoting from the Diagnostic Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder by the American Psychiatric Association; Edward Hudson's Handbook II for Marriage Nullity Cases). Article 36 of the Family Code cannot be taken and construed independently of but must stand in conjunction with, existing precepts in our law on marriage

sources.title: CAROLYN T. MUTYA-SUMILHIG vs. JOSELITO T. SUMILHIG AND REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES
sources.text: Difficult to prove as it may be, a party to a nullity case is still required to prove juridical antecedence because it is an explicit requirement of the law. Article 36 is clear that the psychological incapacity must be "existing at the time of the celebration" of the marriage, "even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after its solemnization." This distinguishes psychological incapacity from divorce. Divorce severs a marital tie even for causes, psychological or otherwise, that may have developed after the marriage celebration.

sources.text:

 The petition is meritorious.

sources.title: REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES vs. LIBERATO P. MOLA CRUZ
sources.text:
In its decision, the CA dismissed the appeal for lack of merit and affirmed the RTC's decision. It reasoned that:

 What matters in cases of declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code is whether the totality of evidence presented is adequate to sustain a finding of psychological incapacity. In the task of ascertaining the presence of psychological incapacity as a ground for the nullity of marriage, the courts, which are concededly not endowed with expertise in the field of psychology, must rely on the opinions of experts in order to inform themselves on the matter, and thus enable themselves to arrive at an intelligent and judicious judgment. Indeed, the conditions for the malady of being grave, antecedent and incurable demand the in-depth diagnosis of experts.

sources.title: G.R. No. 192718 (Supreme Court Decision)
sources.text:
A petition for declaration of nullity of marriage is anchored on Article 36 of the Family Code which provides:

 Art. 36. A marriage contracted by any party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential marital obligation of marriage, shall likewise be void even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after its solemnization. "Psychological incapacity," as a ground to nullify a marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code, should refer to no less than a mental not merely physical incapacity that causes a party to be truly incognitive of the basic marital covenants that concomitantly must be assumed and discharged by the parties to the marriage which, as so expressed in Article 68 of the Family Code, among others, include their mutual obligations to live together; observe love, respect and fidelity; and render help and support. There is hardly a doubt that the intendment of the law has been to confine the meaning of "psychological incapacity" to the most serious cases of personality disorders clearly demonstrative of an utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage.[7](#fnt7)

Based on the provided Philippine legal documents, a clinical or psychiatric evaluation is **no longer mandatory** for the declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code, though courts must still be satisfied that the totality of evidence proves psychological incapacity.

#### 1. Direct Answer & Legal Basis
Under **Article 36 of the Family Code**, a marriage is void if a party was psychologically incapacitated at the time of celebration. While expert opinion is crucial for determining the nature of the incapacity, the Supreme Court has ruled that the personal examination of the defendant by a psychiatrist or psychologist is not strictly required.

> "Even when the rules have been relaxed and the personal examination of the defendant by a psychiatrist or psychologist is no longer mandatory for the declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code..."
> — **G.R. No. 171042** [SOURCE 3]

#### 2. Jurisprudence on Mandatory Evaluation
The Supreme Court has clarified the procedural requirements regarding psychiatric evaluations in nullity cases.

*   **Facts:** In a case involving allegations of psychological incapacity, the petitioner presented evidence including documentary proof and expert reports. The issue was whether a formal personal examination by a psychiatrist was required to sustain the petition.
*   **Issue:** Is a clinical or psychiatric evaluation mandatory to prove psychological incapacity under Article 36?
*   **Ruling:** The Court held that while the rules have been relaxed, the totality of evidence must still prove the gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability of the alleged incapacity.
*   **Doctrine:** The personal examination is no longer mandatory, but the burden of proof remains on the petitioner to demonstrate the three requisites using available evidence.
*   **Practical Meaning:** A party can file a petition for nullity without forcing the other spouse to undergo a psychiatric exam, provided they present sufficient evidence (e.g., expert reports, documentary evidence) that proves the incapacity exists.

#### 3. Requisites for Psychological Incapacity
Even if a formal evaluation is not mandatory, the law requires specific characteristics to be proven regarding the psychological condition.

*   **Gravity:** The incapacity must be serious and grave.
*   **Juridical Antecedence:** The condition must exist at the time of the celebration of the marriage, even if it becomes manifest only after solemnization.
*   **Incurability:** The condition must be medically or clinically permanent or incurable.

> "Psychological incapacity," as a ground to nullify a marriage under Article 36 of the Family Code, should refer to no less than a mental not merely physical incapacity that causes a party to be truly incognitive of the basic marital covenants...
> — **G.R. No. 192718** [SOURCE 8]

#### 4. Role of Expert Opinion
While the *examination* is not mandatory, courts rely on expert opinions to inform their judgment.

*   **Facts:** Courts are not endowed with expertise in psychology and must rely on experts to ascertain the presence of psychological incapacity.
*   **Issue:** How do courts determine the nature of the malady without a formal exam?
*   **Ruling:** The conditions for the malady (grave, antecedent, incurable) demand an in-depth diagnosis of experts.
*   **Doctrine:** Courts must rely on the opinions of experts to arrive at an intelligent and judicious judgment regarding the nature of the psychological condition.
*   **Practical Meaning:** While you do not need to force a spouse into a clinic, presenting a Psychiatric Evaluation Report (like in *Green vs. Green*) strengthens the petition by providing the necessary expert diagnosis.

#### 5. Practical Takeaways for Filing a Petition
If you are considering filing a petition for declaration of nullity of marriage under Article 36:

*   **Evidence Gathering:** Collect documentary evidence proving infidelity, lies, debts, or other behaviors that demonstrate the psychological condition.
*   **Expert Opinion:** Attach a Psychiatric Evaluation Report if available to support the claim of gravity and incurability.
*   **Burden of Proof:** Ensure the totality of evidence presented proves the three requisites (gravity, antecedence, incurability).
*   **Timing:** Be prepared to prove that the incapacity existed at the time of marriage celebration, not just after.

#### 6. Key Legal Distinctions
*   **Mandatory Examination vs. Expert Opinion:** A formal personal examination is *not mandatory*, but expert opinions are highly recommended and often relied upon by courts.
*   **Legal Separation vs. Nullity:** Psychological incapacity leads to nullity (void marriage), whereas abandonment or other causes may lead to legal separation. The requirements for proof differ significantly.

> "The totality of evidence presented during trial by private respondent must still *prove* the gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability of the alleged psychological incapacity."
> — **G.R. No. 171042** [SOURCE 3]
